I shared this story on reddit on March 14, 2017. I contemplated leaving it there, and letting it be lost forever whenever I inevitably nuke my account. It was a hard story for me to type out, and even harder story for me to read and remember.

Begin:

So, today, well yesterday really, I'm celebrating the death of two people. They wouldn't have survived either way, and the quote in the title is around about what was said, but not exactly, as my memory is fuzzy. The person who said it apologized for saying it, but it still stuck with me.

Our first week in Iraq was a bunch of nonsense. We were replacing another until that had been there for like 16 months, and we didn't get any left seat/right seat rides, it was just like, "our replacements are here? fuck you!", so our AO was completely unfamiliar to us, and we didn't have anyone showing us the ropes.

Every day it was another bullshit, gear up, and do nothing mission. We'd come in, gear down, 30 minutes later gear up, and go back out. I was fucking sick of it.

Platoon Sergeant flips on the lights and says "Get it on."

You know what? Fuck this shit. I just laid down. I'm going to take my sweet ass time tying my boots and getting my gear on. Everyone is downstairs maybe 5 minutes before me. I was the driver and had the keys to the Bradley.

It isn't until we're out the gate and I hear the radio chatter that I realize this is the real deal. I fucked up.

By the time we get there it's all over. They already secured the area and CASEVACed the injured. Our crew is tasked with bringing the disabled HMMWV back to the FOB. Or was it Camp? I think we were still calling it a camp back then.

You work around different types of vehicles long enough, you learn the smells. I could smell the difference between a tank, 113, and a Bradley. I could smell the difference between JP8 and gasoline. I could smell the difference between JP8 and.... not JP8... blood.

This HMMWV was Swiss cheese. We were riding around in unarmored HMMWVs at the time. Our gunner hooked it up to the Bradley, and we dragged it about 3 miles back to the FOB.

We unhooked it where maintenance was set up, in the dark of the night. Then we put the Bradley back on the staging line and went back to the building.

The guys who had been in contact were in the showers, full kit, trying to get the blood off.

One of my buddies, best friends, now an NCO, grabs me. Pretty much everyone in the platoon knew that I was slacking getting down to the vehicle. He yells at me, says that basically if they died it was my fault for moving too slow.

The two closest to the blast lost all their limbs. They were basically heads with abdomens attached. I think the Captain still had an arm, as it was described to me. They had no chance to survive.

Still, that stuck with me. I fucked up. It didn't matter whether or not they would've lived, I fucked up when my buddies, family, needed me.

I remember, in his birthday weekend, we both had some DFAC detail, and the same dude said he would cover both our shifts, and he covered neither, so we were drunk as fuck Sunday morning getting the shit smoked out of us.

I remember, before the Stop-Loss kicked in, telling him that I thought that everyone extending to deploy was stupid, and him telling me that he extended. He said that it wasn't about the war, it was about me, SSG P, SGT T, and all of us, because he needed to be there for us.

I wasn't there for him. I was busy tucking in my boot laces because I was "tired".

Yeah, that 5 minutes extra time didn't make a difference, but I fucked up.

I can't finish the story. But yeah, 13 years ago today, I fucked up.

Extra: What sort of make-believe creature would be able to achieve something comparable to humans? What would it look like? Is there a capacity to underwater achievement? Why?
Let's say there was a sea creature (currently existing) with human or slightly higher intelligence. Could it achieve anything comparable to human civilizations? What's the most it could achieve?

No for a couple reasons
First salt water is extraordinarily corrosive (stay with me). This means that any sort of mechanical implements would be limited in scope to the stone age if at all. This would prevent anything I would consider comparable to human civilization.
Second sea creatures don't have hands. Along the same vein this means that tool usage (one of the fundamental aspects of human civilization) along with point one would likely be prevented.
Third ..... no paper. No written tradition. No accumulation of knowledge beyond an oral tradition.
Fourth.... no fire, no agriculture. While the sea is plentiful in resources cordoning off resources to free up labor for specialization could likely not occur. Sea water is full of microbes and smaller fish which would compete for resources if underwater agriculture was tried from an evolutionary standpoint (without significant starting technology).

While it is possible that complex cultures could be created a civilization similar to humans is unlikely due to all the disadvantages of tool use as a biological strategy.
